narrative.title: The Loading Dock Scheduling Audit
narrative.scenario: A distribution hub logs delivery truck arrivals and departures on one operating day, all times in 24-hour codes. A dock frees up only strictly after a truck pulls out — a truck arriving at the exact moment another departs needs its own dock. The yard master wants the smallest dock count that keeps every truck moving without waiting.
narrative.inputFormat: Two integer arrays: arr (arrival times) and dep (departure times), as HHMM codes.
narrative.outputFormat: Return the minimum number of docks (platforms) required.
constraints: A train (truck) arriving at time t cannot share a platform with one departing at t

testCases.explanation: Around 1100, three trucks are simultaneously on-site (950, 1100 arrivals against the 1200 departure).
Each truck departs before the next arrives, so one dock cycles through all three.

starterCode.python:
def find_platforms(arr, dep):
    arr, dep = sorted(arr), sorted(dep)
    i = j = occupied = needed = 0
    while i < len(arr):
        if arr[i] <= dep[j]:     # arrival before (or exactly at) a departure
            occupied += 1
            needed = max(needed, occupied)
            i += 1
        else:
            occupied -= 1
            j += 1
    return needed

hintLevels: Level 1: Sort arrivals and departures independently, then walk them like a merge — the running count is dock occupancy.
Level 2: `<=` on arrival vs departure encodes the same-instant rule: equality forces a new dock.
Level 3: The peak of the occupancy trace is the answer; sorting decouples events from their trains.
